newsitem.title: USA: U.S. soy yield better than expected despite stress.
newsitem.headline: U.S. soy yield better than expected despite stress.

text.p: Early harvested U.S. soybean fields were producing better than expected yields despite below normal summer temperatures and a dry spell in August, agronomists and grain merchandisers said.

"Reflecting back on the weather pattern of (this summer) it's amazing to me that the plants have been able to produce the seed size they've managed to produce," said Gary Pepper, a University of Illinois extension agronomist.
"The yields are not extremely disappointing but they've been better in other years," he added.
Early planted fields near Champaign-Urbana, Illinois, were yielding 40 to 50 bushels per acre (bpa), Pepper said. Illinois's soybean yield was 38.5 bpa last year.
USDA in its September 11 crop report pegged U.S. soybean yield at 35.8 bpa, compared with 34.9 bpa in 1995.
Last week's rains slowed harvest which remained behind average pace, Illinois's Agricultural Statistics Service said.

"The weather pattern here the last few days has been very conducive to drying the crop," Pepper said. "They're going to move into harvest-ready condition almost faster than the farmer can get to them."
Four percent of the crop had been harvested as of Sunday, trailing the average of 18 percent.

In Iowa, traditionally the leading U.S. soybean producer, yields were mostly in the 40 bpa range, said Iowa State University extension agronomist Dale Farnham. Last year, Iowa produced an average of 43 bpa.
The crop was one percent harvested as of Sunday and 66 percent was dropping leaves, Iowa's statistical service said.
Most of the harvest activity was concentrated in central and southwest Iowa, said Bill Bluml, assistant marketing manager for West Central Cooperative in Ralston, Iowa.
"I thought maybe there would be better yields in some areas but it's still too early to tell," he said.
Farmers were reluctant to sell newly harvested crops after CBOT futures fell sharply on Monday, he said.
"There's a certain amount that has been sold already but with the big break in prices, we haven't seen a lot of farmers selling," he said.
In Indiana, early harvested fields in White, Cass, Clinton and Carroll counties were yielding more than 60 bpa, said Purdue University agronomist Ellsworth Christmas.
"This is an area that got planted pretty well on time and has had very good rainfall all summer long," he said.
The crop was three percent harvested as of Sunday, compared with an average 20 percent, and 20 percent was mature.

But elsewhere in the state where late planting and irregular rainfall stressed the crops, yield projections were less promising. Christmas estimated the state would yield an average of 35 bpa. Many pods contained two beans instead of the normal three, he said.
"It could come in lower than (35 bpa) but I certainly don't expect it to come in any higher than that," he said.
--Chicago Newsdesk 312-408-8749
